lst2.title: Listening 2
lst2.script:
Part One

My name is Huda. Our class had been learning about Communication when a practical problem changed how I understood the subject. We were exploring a bilingual student news bulletin and had planned to meet at the media room at a school in Sohar. I was pleased to join because I wanted to practise communicating with people whose experiences were different from mine.

The challenge began when a meeting notice appeared with the correct day but the wrong room. I did not want to make a quick judgement, particularly because an incorrect assumption could affect other people. I told the English teacher what had happened and asked how to check the available information. We agreed that finding the cause was more important than looking for somebody to blame.

After listening to different suggestions, she compared the notice with the booking records and spoke to the organiser. We used a microphone and a shared editing computer and compared our first impression with a comparison of the original audio and two rewritten captions. The group also spoke to a local radio volunteer for a second opinion. That conversation showed me why a confident explanation is not always a reliable explanation.

Part Two

Several pupils were unsure whether our approach would work. Their concern was understandable because some families preferred printed notices to phone messages. We considered those doubts and checked which steps were practical. I learnt that listening respectfully to an alternative view can strengthen a plan rather than delay it.

Eventually, the team used one official noticeboard and a matching website update. We reported the result to the people who had helped us and invited feedback. The discussion included asking speakers for permission before publishing their voices, because completing a successful project should never mean ignoring another person's rights or safety.

Looking back, I believe clear communication depends on checking meaning rather than simply sending more messages. The experience has changed the way I approach group work. We are now hoping to prepare a workshop on clear spoken and written messages, but first we will review the evidence again. I feel more able to ask questions and make careful decisions in an unfamiliar situation.

At every stage, the students checked a comparison of the original audio and two rewritten captions before making a public claim about the results. Several family members said that a workshop on clear spoken and written messages would make the project useful beyond the first event. Teachers encouraged the group to discuss some families preferred printed notices to phone messages and respect people whose priorities were different.

lst2.script:
Part One

My name is Ali. Our class had been learning about Tourism and Hospitality when a practical problem changed how I understood the subject. We were exploring an accessible welcome programme for visitors and had planned to meet at a training hotel near Salalah. I was pleased to join because I wanted to practise communicating with people whose experiences were different from mine.

The challenge began when a visitor's excursion was cancelled when a mountain road became unsafe after rain. I did not want to make a quick judgement, particularly because an incorrect assumption could affect other people. I told a hospitality instructor what had happened and asked how to check the available information. We agreed that finding the cause was more important than looking for somebody to blame.

After listening to different suggestions, he explained the options calmly and organised a safer coastal alternative. We used an accessible map and multilingual welcome cards and compared our first impression with visitor comments, route inspections and a review of reception questions. The group also spoke to an experienced hotel receptionist for a second opinion. That conversation showed me why a confident explanation is not always a reliable explanation.

Part Two

Several pupils were unsure whether our approach would work. Their concern was understandable because some travellers preferred independent routes with no fixed schedule. We considered those doubts and checked which steps were practical. I learnt that listening respectfully to an alternative view can strengthen a plan rather than delay it.

Eventually, the group enjoyed the day and thanked the staff for honest advice. We reported the result to the people who had helped us and invited feedback. The discussion included protecting personal information and respecting local cultural practices, because completing a successful project should never mean ignoring another person's rights or safety.

Looking back, I believe good hospitality combines clear information, inclusion and respect for visitors. The experience has changed the way I approach group work. We are now hoping to prepare a community-led guide to responsible tourism in Dhofar, but first we will review the evidence again. I feel more able to ask questions and make careful decisions in an unfamiliar situation.

The project showed the value of checking information, explaining decisions clearly and inviting feedback. It also demonstrated that transport decisions require reliable evidence, safety and consideration for different travellers, a principle that applies to many situations beyond the original setting. The participants returned to a transport meeting in Sohar with clearer questions and a better understanding of the original challenge. At every stage, the students checked a month of journey logs comparing waiting times on different routes before making a public claim about the results. Several family members said that a small mobile timetable with accessibility information would make the project useful beyond the first event.
